claims.text: Titanium alloys with a high volume fraction of equiaxed alpha grains will exhibit enhanced ductility.
The enhanced ductility is caused by grain boundary-mediated plasticity.
The initial material is a polycrystalline titanium alloy containing alpha and beta phases.
Hot rolling followed by recrystallization annealing can control the titanium alloy microstructure.
The recrystallization annealing treatment is performed at 900°C for 2 hours.
Ductility is evaluated at room temperature and a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Grain boundaries and dislocation density are the structural mediators of the ductility response.
Grain boundaries act as sinks for dislocations.
Dislocation absorption at grain boundaries reduces stress concentrations.
Reduced stress concentration promotes ductile deformation.
The processed alloy will have 25% greater elongation to failure than the baseline.
The baseline elongation to failure is 15%.
The baseline is a conventional titanium alloy with a lamellar microstructure.
The target elongation to failure is greater than 18.75%.
The magnitude of ductility enhancement may depend on alloy composition and processing conditions.
Mechanisms other than grain boundary-mediated plasticity may contribute to the ductility response.

contradictions.description: A 25% increase from a 15% baseline equals exactly 18.75%, whereas the stated success boundary requires elongation to be strictly greater than 18.75%.

The boundary requires elongation greater than 18.75%, but the falsification rule rejects only values below 18.75%; a result exactly equal to 18.75% would neither meet the boundary nor falsify the hypothesis.
